newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italian lira set to rejoin Europe's ERM.
newsitem.headline: Italian lira set to rejoin Europe's ERM.

text.p: Italy's hopes of joining a common European currency in 1999 are likely to be bolstered on Saturday when officials meet to consider the lira's return to the European Union's system of semi-fixed exchange rates.
After an absence of more four years, the Italian government Friday formally asked its EU partners to rejoin the grid that links 11 of the 15 member nations' currencies.

A meeting of the EU's monetary committee was set for Brussels on Saturday to decide the rate at which the lira would come back in. A stable two year-stint within the currency grid is one of the criteria for countries wishing to join the single currency.

Both Italy and Britain were forced out of the grid in 1992 after a currency crisis nearly brought the system to its knees. Should Italy return to the grid this weekend, only three nations, Britain, Sweden and Greece, would remain outside.

The Italian government does not want the lira to re-enter the grid at too high a level because of the adverse effect on its exports. Neighbour France, however, wants it in at a less competitive rate because of the impact on their own industry.
One EU diplomat Friday predicted intense negotiations.
"It will be a difficult meeting," he said.
Another said bargaining over the central rate would likely begin at around the levels currently seen in foreign exchange markets. The lira traded between 995 and 1,000 to the German mark on Friday.

German concerns over the future credibility of a single currency have been voiced repeatedly in recent months, punctuated by fears that politics will be the overriding factor in deciding which countries join economic and monetary union in 1999.

European countries that want to include their currencies in the planned Euro from 1999 are rushing to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in 1997 -- necessary if they are to be at the start.

Most are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of 3 percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Several governments, including Italy, have used controversial one-time budget measures to bring their deficits under control.

But some EU monetary officials said that while Italy's turbulent currency history may be a reason to pause, it has nevertheless made enormous strides in recent years towards becoming a more stable and prosperous economy.
Such an effort cannot be simply brushed aside, they said.
